analysis.one_liner: Provides federal grants so states can guarantee affordable, comprehensive health insurance to everyone.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in the House and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a two-phase federal program: first, states could take federal money to cover residents earning up to three times the poverty level through a public benefit package modeled on the plan offered to federal employees; then, by 2008, every state would have to cover everyone. Premiums and out-of-pocket costs would be capped by income, employers would have to pay at least 80% of premiums, insurance plans would have to spend at least 90% of premiums on actual care, and Medicare would get full mental health coverage. It was introduced in July 2002 with one cosponsor, referred to two House committees, and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 38.7 million uninsured Americans counted in the bill's findings — more than half of them in working families earning under three times the poverty line — would gain guaranteed coverage with premiums and cost-sharing capped by income, no preexisting-condition exclusions, and a benefit package at least as rich as the federal employees' plan. Low- and middle-income workers who pay rising premiums would pay less, since employers would have to cover at least 80% of premiums. Medicare beneficiaries would gain full mental health and substance abuse coverage, and the 31 million people facing medical-bill collections each year would be protected.

how_it_helps.text: States would receive federal matching grants to cover residents earning up to 300% of the poverty line, with premiums capped at 3% of family income and cost-sharing at 5%, and no premiums at all for families under 150% of poverty [S2, S3].

Coverage would be as good as the Federal Employees Health Benefits standard Blue Cross/Blue Shield preferred provider plan, including mental health parity, with no preexisting-condition exclusions [S3].

By 2008 every state would have to cover 100% of eligible residents; employers would have to contribute at least 80% of premiums (capped at 10% of wages) through state purchasing pools, and workers could sue employers that retaliated against them [S3].

Medicare enrollees would get full mental health and substance abuse parity, and the bill added consumer protections: disclosure of provider financial arrangements, notice of facility closures and mergers, continued coverage during plan disruptions, and home care standards [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on the federal budget through open-ended appropriations (the bill says it should be offset by budget surpluses, health savings, or limits on tax benefits for top-bracket individuals and corporations), and partly on employers, who would owe at least 80% of employee premiums up to 10% of payroll. Private insurers would face a 90% minimum medical-loss requirement, an annual competitive bidding process for state purchasing pools, and loss of ERISA preemption shielding their employer-group plans from state regulation and lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The bill was an open-ended federal spending commitment — 'such sums as may be necessary' each year, as direct budget authority — with no identified revenue source beyond a non-binding 'sense of Congress' that it be paid for out of budget surpluses, health savings, or limits on tax benefits for top-bracket individuals and corporations [S3].

The employer mandate (80% of premiums, capped at 10% of wages) would have raised labor costs for businesses, particularly smaller firms, and the private right of action with liquidated damages and attorney's fees would have created new litigation exposure for employers [S3].

States were required to submit plans and comply on a federal timetable, with residents allowed to sue a state in federal court if it failed to submit an approved plan — a significant shift of authority from states to the federal government [S3].

By waiving ERISA preemption, the bill opened employer health plans to state regulation and lawsuits, which employers and insurers argued would raise costs and cause some employers to drop coverage [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit was large — guaranteed coverage for tens of millions of uninsured people, lower cost-sharing for working families, and lower administrative overhead — but the bill's cost was also enormous and never officially estimated: an open-ended federal entitlement, funded by unspecified surplus revenues and tax-limitation language that had not been scored. Critics would also note that states were forced into a federally prescribed system, employers faced new contribution mandates and litigation exposure, and the bill did not contain a stable, identified funding source. Had it reached the floor, the honest debate would have been between real coverage gains and a very large, permanent federal spending commitment with uncertain financing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with one cosponsor, sent to two House committees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 26, 2002, and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees; no markup, hearing, or vote is recorded in the action history [S5].
On July 29, 2002 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health in Energy and Commerce, where it sat for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
Only one House member, Rep. David Obey (D-WI), cosponsored the bill, and it had no Senate companion in the record provided [S4].
The bill received no further action before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and all bills not enacted die at the end of a Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the groups that would have borne its costs are better off: large employers facing a new premium mandate and litigation exposure, and insurers facing overhead caps and state purchasing pools. The roughly 39 million uninsured gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers spared the mandate

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were House Democrats, and the bill received no action in a House controlled by 223 Republicans, so the process split along party lines even though no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill capped administrative spending and profits (at least 90% of premium dollars had to go to care) and channeled coverage through state-run purchasing pools with annual competitive bidding, squeezing insurers' overhead and margins. The FEHBP-style benefit benchmark also offered rich coverage at regulated cost-sharing.
Employers would have had to pay at least 80% of premiums (capped at 10% of payroll) and lose ERISA's shield from state health regulation and employee lawsuits, raising costs and litigation exposure.

industries.industry: Health care providers and health care workers
industries.note: Universal coverage would have brought tens of millions of new insured patients, reducing uncompensated care, while staffing standards, disclosure rules, and worker protections (notice of closures, right of first refusal, anti-unionization funding limits) strengthened health workers' position.
